source_document.body:
When Integrated Business Planning (IBP) is established effectively, it gives leaders something every company needs: one practical way to align demand, supply, finance and operations. It creates discipline, exposes trade-offs and helps the business work from a shared view of the plan.
What’s Related
The challenge is that today’s operating environment moves faster than the traditional IBP cycle. Demand changes, suppliers miss commitments, costs shift, and geopolitical events create new constraints. Yet many teams still spend weeks gathering data , reconciling assumptions and preparing presentations. By the time a decision is made, the situation may have changed.
In my conversations with executives, three questions come up repeatedly.
1. What should IBP become?
The answer is not another dashboard. It is also not simply compressing a monthly process into a weekly one. Running the same process more frequently does not necessarily produce faster or better decisions.
IBP needs to move from orchestrating meetings to orchestrating decisions. Instead of waiting for the calendar, the process should respond when a meaningful event occurs.
Agentic AI can help enable that shift. Intelligent agents can monitor changes in demand, supply, inventory, capacity and financial performance. When a significant change occurs, they can evaluate alternatives and recommend a response. Routine actions can be executed within established limits, while higher-risk decisions can be escalated to planners or executives.
This changes the purpose of the management business review. Leaders should spend less time reconciling yesterday’s numbers and more time governing policies, resolving strategic trade-offs and addressing the exceptions that genuinely require judgment.
RELATED: Supply Chain 101: Why Demand Planning Is Crucial for Business Success
2. How much autonomy is realistic?
“Autonomous” does not mean that every planning decision should be handed to a machine. Decisions vary in value, complexity and risk.
A routine inventory transfer may be suitable for automated execution. A decision involving a strategic customer, a constrained product or significant financial exposure may still require leadership approval.
“IBP needs to move from orchestrating meetings to orchestrating decisions. Instead of waiting for the calendar, the process should respond when a meaningful event occurs.”
The objective should not be maximum automation. It should be the right level of automation for each decision, supported by transparency, accountability and clear escalation paths.
I believe autonomy must be earned one decision at a time. Companies should begin with decisions that occur frequently, have measurable economic value and can be governed within clear boundaries. In one global consumer products organization, a decision intelligence layer was implemented to identify excess and shortage inventory across distribution centers , evaluate the cost and service implications of transfers, and generate stock-transfer recommendations as part of the supply plan. The process included accept, reject, and review controls, while service-critical transfers were automated as autonomous decisions within guardrails defined and periodically updated through the IBP process.
They can then test the recommendations, validate the financial logic and build trust before expanding the level of autonomy.
That is a more credible path than launching a broad technology program before the organization has agreed on how decisions should be made.
3. How do you make the case to a skeptical board?
A compelling vision for the future of IBP will not, by itself, secure investment. Boards and CEOs rarely approve a transformation because the technology sounds impressive. They want to understand the value, the risk and the path to results.
The business case should therefore begin with value leakage, not software features.
Where are slow or inconsistent decisions causing premium freight , excess inventory, obsolescence, lost sales, service failures or unnecessary manual work? Which decisions are contributing to those outcomes? How would a different IBP operating model improve them?
The value can be explained through three lenses.
Cost and productivity: reducing expediting, excess inventory, planning effort and avoidable operational disruption .
Revenue and margin protection: responding faster to demand changes, allocating constrained supply more intelligently and protecting service for priority products and customers.
Resilience : identifying disruption earlier, evaluating choices faster and recovering with less volatility.
The value does not need to depend on a fully autonomous process. For example, an AI/ML-enabled inventory optimization program at a global automotive manufacturer combined machine-learning forecasting , external-factor sensing, segmentation, and simulation to improve forecast accuracy by 30% and reduce inventory by $77 million, while eliminating 1.7 million cubic feet of required storage space. In another example, a life sciences manufacturer achieved 90% touchless demand planning , 85% touchless supply planning and 90% touchless inventory planning, contributing to a 10% inventory reduction, a 30% productivity improvement and a 20% forecast accuracy improvement.
A credible case must also acknowledge what the transformation requires. The investment may include the technology platform, data foundation, integration, process redesign, governance, change management and workforce capabilities. Leaving those elements out may make the headline return look better, but it also makes the proposal less believable.
The roadmap should be staged, with clear value targets and decision points for scaling, adjusting or stopping. This gives the board visibility into results without asking it to approve an open-ended technology bet.
The question leaders should ask
The future of IBP will be increasingly event-driven, financially informed and human-governed. Monthly reviews will remain important, but they will no longer carry the full weight of enterprise decision-making.
The question for CEOs and boards is not, “How much AI should we add to IBP?” A more useful question is, “Which decisions must improve, what value will that create and what capabilities will allow us to proceed with confidence?”
The original IBP model brought discipline to planning. Its next evolution must bring greater speed and adaptability without sacrificing accountability.
IBP will not disappear as a monthly process. But the decisions that matter will no longer wait for the next monthly meeting.
Ehap Sabri is the Supply Chain Software Alliances Leader & SC Planning Co-Leader at EY Americas. The views reflected in this article are the views of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of Ernst & Young LLP or other members of the global EY organization.
